children: Apple
unveiled its long-awaited foldable iPhone on Wednesday, marking its entrance into a market currently dominated by Samsung
, Alphabet's Google
, and Lenovo's Motorola
, with China's Xiaomi
and Huawei also launching models this week.
So how important is the new foldable iPhone to Apple's
future?
Seeking Alpha analysts
, and
weigh in.
The Curious Analyst: I think the foldable iPhone is important to Apple
. But I wouldn’t treat it as a make-or-break kind of product.
In my view, its biggest value is that it gives Apple
a new premium price tier above the Pro lineup. This could definitely lift average selling prices and improve mix even if first-year volumes are modest. I think it also gives Apple
another reason to accelerate the replacement cycle across its more than 2.5B active users, especially as AI features become more deeply integrated into the hardware experience.
That said, I'm seeing it as more of an earnings and ecosystem catalyst as opposed to a unit-volume increase. And the benefits could extend to suppliers such as Broadcom
and Qualcomm
. At the end of the day, I think the foldable could become a meaningful contributor to EPS growth over the next few years.
Valuation Rewind: We would be very cautious here, since Apple
is entering an existing category rather than creating a new one, as it effectively did with the modern smartphone. Foldables still account for only around 2% of smartphone sales, despite Samsung
already being on its eighth generation. That tells us consumers have not been fascinated enough by the concept itself to make it mainstream.
We clearly stated in our recent article
Apple: The Winter Is Coming
that we view the iPhone as a form of affordable luxury. With household savings rates already stretched, Apple
now appears ready to introduce an even more expensive device positioned well above the Pro Max and firmly in the ultra-premium segment.
For that reason, we do not think the fact that the iPhone folds is, by itself, revolutionary enough to trigger another major upgrade cycle. Apple
would have to surprise us with genuinely new functionality, something users did not even know they needed, rather than simply offer a larger screen that folds into a pocket.
If that happens and Apple
truly surprises us, it could make us question our bearish thesis. If not, our bearish thesis would only strengthen.
Damon Verial: The foldable iPhone doesn't matter much as a product itself, but for revenue generation it could bring a lot of value.

Now, foldables have been around for seven years and have yet to gain significant traction. Only about 2% of smartphones worldwide are foldables. To be fair, I have a foldable and love it. But investors should be aware that this category of smartphone isn't a revolution, even if Apple
has now joined the "trend."

That said, this specific foldable phone certainly is arriving at a great time: Apple posted lowered guidance in July due to the AI-spurred rationing of DRAM and NAND. To compensate, the company has been raising prices. A new premium phone is possibly the best use of those scarce gigabytes left to convert into novel products, especially now that the iPhone 18 has been pushed back to the spring.

The foldable will also be John Ternus's first launch as CEO after literally one week on the job. I think it makes for a pretty good story for investors: a hardware engineer steps up amidst a supply crunch and ships a new category of phone. It's also the first shot against Samsung's
seven-year monopoly on premium foldables.
Overall, Apple
, along with Micron
and SK Hynix
, seems to be one of the companies making the best decisions during this memory squeeze. I remain bullish on Apple, selling shorts as per my recent article on the company.
